member of the commission. − mr president, mr perello rodriguez asked the commission to look into new ways of financing ccs. we are doing that, but actually several possibilities for financing this technology already exist in the eu. i mentioned some of them in my opening remarks. it is fair to say that the problem here is not a lack of eu funding; the problem has been that a number of member states have either been slow in prioritising between different ccs demonstration projects and/or have come up with inadequate national co-financing. with regard to the discussion about whether we are putting too much emphasis on ccs and what it can and cannot do, i would agree with those who warn that we should not think it can make a disproportionately big contribution. we should not overestimate it. but i would also say that those of us who want ambitious climate policies have to ask ourselves whether we can really afford to kill off potentially interesting technologies in their infancy. i do not think we can. i think we will need all the technologies we can come up with. that is why it basically depends on whether the eu gets its act together in developing this technology and others. we must explore the realistic potential; we need to know the realistic potential, including on a large scale. that is the first thing that needs to be addressed when we talk about ccs. then, of course, we need to recognise that it is only one element in a range of technologies and a range of things on our to-do list when it comes to reducing the carbon footprint.
member of the commission. − mr president, firstly i would like to thank mr gerbrandy and all the members of the european parliament. i am grateful for your initiative to bring the issue of wildlife trafficking to the attention of parliament and the other institutions. the world is facing a dramatic surge in wildlife trafficking, which has become one of the most profitable criminal activities at global level. it threatens the survival of some emblematic species, damages biodiversity and undermines the development and stability of many countries. we will begin to tackle this successfully only if there is a joint international effort involving source, transit and destination countries. the european union has been working towards this for some time, both domestically and through cites, the international convention that regulates trade in endangered species. i take this opportunity to let you know that the commission has recently tabled a proposal for the european union finally to become a full party to cites. we hope parliament will be able to give its consent before the elections. we also raise the question of wildlife trafficking in our bilateral cooperation exchanges. just last summer, for example, i signed a cooperation agreement on wildlife trafficking with my chinese counterpart, and we are also supporting the efforts of cites and 31 african elephant-range states with extra funding from the 10th european development fund (edf). in december we announced eur 12.3 million for the new ‘mikes’ project. mikes stands for ‘minimising the illegal killing of elephants and other endangered species’. it will develop law enforcement, monitoring, patrol and emergency response capacities to fight illegal killing and international trade in elephants and other species. however, we have to face the fact that the trends are against us. demand for wildlife products in asia is now so big that the business is highly lucrative. for example, rhino horn is more expensive than cocaine and gold; at the same time, it is easy to smuggle, the risk of detection is very low, and sanctions, if imposed, are often not sufficient to act as a deterrent. ivory trafficking has boomed and is now affecting the whole continent of africa. the european union itself is a market and a transit point for illegal wildlife products. for many countries, wildlife crime is a threat to development. corruption facilitates trafficking, and large-scale organised crime undermines weak state structures and threatens peace and stability. to begin to turn this situation around, we need much greater political recognition of the threat that wildlife trafficking represents. this needs to go far beyond environmental circles: foreign ministers, organised-crime and development experts, police and customs, the judiciary, ngos and the private sector all have an important role to play. your draft resolution addresses many of the key issues at stake and calls for enhanced action. a number of member states and the united states of america have recently announced that they will increase their political engagement against wildlife trafficking. the commission is working on a set of ideas for how the european union could develop a more effective approach in the fight against wildlife trafficking. we will present those ideas, including in relation to opportunities offered by the new edf, next month in a commission communication to parliament and the member states, on which i am taking the lead together with commissioner malmström and in close cooperation with other commissioners, notably commissioner piebalgs. the communication will draw attention to the urgency of addressing the global problem of wildlife trafficking more effectively. it takes stock of existing european union measures to support the fight against wildlife trafficking both globally and within the union. finally, it will initiate a debate on the european union’s future approach to wildlife trafficking. the dimensions of the problem, as i indicated earlier, have changed, so new ideas are needed to fight organised wildlife crime, curb demand, address the peace and stability implications and provide for alternative livelihoods for those involved in poaching. we will therefore ask stakeholders for their views as to what has been working well and what has been working less well, and we will explore avenues for more effective action by the european union. in addition to the public consultation, we will organise a conference on 10 april 2014. parliament’s resolution is a very helpful contribution to raising public awareness of the importance of this issue. commissioner malmström and i look forward to the discussion with you and many other stakeholders on potential solutions to ensure that we are up to the challenge of fighting wildlife trafficking effectively.
for the greens/efa group mr president, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, this oral question and the resolution which we are discussing tonight and which we will be voting on this week, i hope by a very large majority, is a political appeal and response to a serious and growing international problem, as my colleagues have pointed out. the trafficking of wildlife is now the fourth largest trade in the world, behind illicit drugs, human trafficking and arms trafficking. unep and interpol estimate that this crime generates between 18 and 26 billion euros annually. almost two-thirds of forest elephants in central africa were killed between 2002 and 2012 for their ivory for the illegal market. the killing of hundreds of elephants in cameroon in early 2012 by heavily armed gangs from sudan illustrates a dramatic situation. in recent decades, criminal networks have become increasingly aggressive in their search for natural products. tiger teeth, bear bile, rhino horns, bird feathers, shark fins, coral and turtle shells - no species is truly spared from the world's biodiversity pirates. today, the consequences of poaching and illegal wildlife trade go beyond the conservation of biodiversity. they affect the security, governance and integrity of many states and populations. several studies indicate that these activities are fuelling organised crime worldwide, that they are involved in money laundering, corruption, the purchase of weapons of war and the operation of rebel and even terrorist groups. this is a trade that has already reportedly caused over 1,000 deaths among the environmental guards charged with protecting wildlife with repercussions for local populations and entire regions. this crime is becoming nothing less than a serious threat to peace and security. interpol and other international bodies are calling on police forces worldwide to tackle environmental damage, and on all states to strengthen their laws and enforcement of sanctions against these criminal networks. if environmental damage and biodiversity loss have not been enough to move citizens and the international community, things can and must change as we begin 2014. as the european territory is the main transit and destination area for this traffic, the european parliament has taken stock of the challenge and its responsibility. that is the subject of our resolution. the european union must have serious and effective tools. the member states must harmonize their laws and strengthen their customs services. we call on the commission and the council to take action, as a priority on the eu agenda, and for europol to be involved. we call for zero tolerance to effectively combat the scourge of wildlife crime.

the rapporteur. - mr president, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, it is a real pleasure to be debating with you this morning the agreement our institutions have reached on this subject, an agreement which has required more than two years of negotiations. i would like to make it clear that although the consumer programme is often presented as a small programme in view of its budget, less than eur 200 million over the seven years to 2020, it is nevertheless a great responsibility for the union. consumption, i remind you, is 50% of the union's gross domestic product and, in this period when we are looking for growth, it is far from negligible. how has the text evolved since it was tabled by the commission and where are we today? first of all, i would like to thank the commission because its text was a good starting point, but we wanted to give it new and complementary political impetus. in conclusion, and on the substance, i would say that we have essentially made three major changes that have led to three real breakthroughs. first, we have turned this programme towards the future. it is a question of defining the guidelines until 2020 and, to be more specific, i would like to say that in the area of safety, for example, we have strengthened the aspects related to the traceability of products. as far as consumer information is concerned, we have stressed the need for market transparency and the comparability of information and data. in the field of education, we propose to make more intensive and effective use of the possibilities offered by new technologies, online platforms, machine translations, etc. finally, as regards appeals, and god knows how important this is in consumer disputes, we are putting the package on the extrajudicial dispute settlement mechanisms and i am thinking in particular of the introduction of the electronic odr platform, which i believe will offer consumers new possibilities. however, this odr platform for out-of-court online dispute resolution is a major and important project that will have to be realized. secondly, we have strengthened and clarified the type of support to be offered to the actors on the ground, to those who, at the grassroots level, in the territories, in the member states, are working to ensure that this consumer protection is effective. this support will be expressed in the form of training for member states' agents, focusing mainly on risk assessment, increased support for european consumer centres, direct financial means for consumer organisations at european level, because behind these programmes we must recognise the work of the activists, those who are closest to consumers on a daily basis. thirdly, i would say that we have included this programme in the continuity taking into account the economic context of the crisis and the demographic changes in consumer behaviour. with the exponential and spectacular growth of online commerce, with consumers saturated with information, with increasing complexity in decision-making, we wanted, in this context, to highlight the development of reliable online comparison sites for consumers, taking into account not only prices but also the quality of goods and services, because this is essential to be part of the ecological evolution and the rejection of waste, which is indispensable. finally, let me say in conclusion that we have included a point, which was the final point of our discussions, on which we have reached agreement - and i welcome this - on the monitoring and evaluation of this programme. in september 2017, we will make a milestone which will be followed, if necessary, by a legislative proposal to ensure that the second part of the programme is adapted if necessary. so let me conclude by thanking the successive presidencies, in particular the cypriot and lithuanian ones, and also warmly thanking my colleagues the fictitious rapporteurs, and tell you that it is confidence in the markets that we are going to strengthen by guaranteeing and strengthening consumer rights.

in writing. france is the sixth scientific power in the world and yet it is only in fifteenth place in terms of innovation. innovation, boldness and anticipation will make our companies, our regions and our country competitive. the deterioration of our position vis-à-vis our main trading partner, germany, and vis-à-vis the major emerging powers must prompt us to react immediately and to develop strategies to regain world markets. in this spirit, the structural funds must help the regions and the country to move towards growth by concentrating investment on ambitious and promising projects. the reform of cohesion policy integrates this approach with the smart specialisation strategy. regions must highlight their strengths and exploit their potential in research, development and innovation. as in the silicon valley near grenoble, we must encourage regions to become centres of excellence and competitiveness and develop new projects. obviously, such an ambition can only emerge by bringing together actors from the world of business, research and academia, and not just the usual institutional actors who are not used to taking risks.
in writing. it is a report that calls for regions to 'smart specialisation', i.e. competition without limits. it is part of the horizon 2020 vision on research, development and innovation, which aims to a large extent to develop knowledge only where it is of interest to the private sector. the 'poles of competitiveness' advocated are part of this logic. it encourages the regions to develop their strengths in certain areas while including civil society as much as possible and asking them to keep in mind the need to address societal challenges such as the fight against unemployment and poverty, the energy transition or reindustrialisation. this report has no legislative value and no substance, it is a liberal manifesto. i vote against it.
in writing. this strategy aims to optimise the use of european funds dedicated to regional policy. it is based on the strengths and comparative advantages of each region, and it will have to invest european funds mainly in these areas. the aim is therefore to exploit the regional potential and thus to conquer areas which can offer high economic added value and create jobs. i therefore voted in favour of this report.
in writing. what is meant by "intelligent specialisation"? these are simply national or regional innovation strategies which aim to create a competitive advantage by developing and matching research and innovation strengths with business needs in order to take advantage of new opportunities and market developments, or more simply: to streamline skills as much as possible to get the most out of them. in practice, it is not just a question of betting on innovation at any cost, but of organising it around other priorities, such as the fight against unemployment, poverty or the security of energy supplies. the guidelines set out in this report are in line with this, which is why i supported it by voting in the plenary.

in writing. as transport is one of the largest emitters of greenhouse gases, the european union and car manufacturers have undertaken to reduce these emissions gradually. the krahmer report is in line with this and sets an ambitious and reasonable target for new commercial vehicles by 2020: 147g co2 / km. in addition, the target range of between 105g and 120g co2/km by 2025 creates predictability for manufacturers. the compromise is good for both the climate and the car manufacturers, so i voted in favour of the text.

in writing. i voted in favour of this report on the reduction of co2 emissions from new light commercial vehicles. the european union needs to address this issue as failure to determine or implement the modalities would have a detrimental impact on car manufacturers and spare parts suppliers. the latter need certainty about the technology and vehicles needed to meet environmental objectives. this text meets the expectations of the various actors while preserving the environment, and i welcome this compromise.
in writing. i voted in favour of this agreement, which will encourage the reduction of co2 emissions from light commercial vehicles while preserving the competitiveness of our automotive industry. i am pleased that the already very ambitious 2020 reduction targets have been retained and that the long-term targets are not binding. the european car manufacturers are being hit hard by the economic crisis and it is necessary not to put them at a competitive disadvantage vis-à-vis their foreign competitors. new tests will also be introduced to measure co2 emissions and fuel consumption more effectively. this will help to inform consumers, including the many smes for whom commercial vehicles are a crucial work tool and a major expense.
in writing. from 2020, vans sold in the european union will have to emit 28% less co2 than current standards. the emission threshold of 147g co2 per km instead of 203g/km today is a widely achievable threshold which should not be a burden for the automotive industry. this objective represents an average of the emissions permitted for each manufacturer, which can offset the emissions of their most polluting models with their own models. beyond the environmental objective, this decision is an opportunity to unleash creative energies and to encourage the automotive industry to develop new models with advanced technology to make it a competitive and innovative industry. this is a major challenge for the sector, which was hit hard by the crisis in 2008. the electric car project developed by renault-nissan and navia, this fully electric automated transport developed by a french company, induct, demonstrates how much france is full of visionary and daring minds. let us therefore ensure that these initiatives are encouraged, valued and exploited, both at eu and national level.
in writing. the text is set in a clearly liberal, productivist and free-trade framework which we know all too well. the rapporteurs could have made the effort to lower the level of emissions for 2020 and not for 2025 and taken the text out of its free-trade box, to actually change the terms. for these reasons, it is difficult to vote without reservation. however, it is very clear that the rapporteurs have shed light on some issues, in particular the false underestimation of co2 emissions from commercial vehicles or the real flaws in the current calculation methods: the answer is clear, the administration will have to rely on a more realistic calculation method, in particular from the international methods seems more reliable. the rapporteur also proposes to take into account the whole life cycle of vehicles, up to recycling. these are coercive measures, not merely declaratory, which may produce real effects, although they are clearly insufficient. i abstain to encourage these good resolutions.
in writing. this report concerns carbon dioxide emissions from new light commercial vehicles. while denouncing the fact that manufacturers underestimate the co2 emissions of their vehicles - which is a good thing - it proposes to confirm the target of 147g co2/km by 2020 and to raise it to between 105 and 120g co2/km by 2025. the report justifies these long delays in particular by the current economic situation which does not allow car manufacturers to make the necessary investments and smes to pay more for these vehicles (these standards resulting in a surcharge of up to 10%). while the strengthening of these thresholds is good news, i regret that the deadlines are so unambitious. the difficult economic situation behind this report is only the consequence of austerity policies that curb investment, which has a direct impact on our health and our environment. however, as the way forward is to tighten up these standards, i have chosen to abstain.
in writing. preserving our natural environment is rightly one of the european union's top priorities. we must act now to preserve the vast resources of our planet. this report should therefore be adopted. the co2 reduction targets in this report are ambitious, but achievable. it was important to keep 2020 as the reference year both for feasibility and for the protection of manufacturers. while protecting the environment is imperative, we must bear in mind that, as in the automobile sector, commercial vehicle manufacturers need safety, especially in this time of crisis. so it is important to avoid imposing unrealistic expectations on them. we must take steps and not get bogged down in unrealistic practices.
in writing. as part of the strategy to reduce co2 emissions from light vehicles in 2011, the eu adopted a regulation that targets co2 emissions from new light commercial vehicles sold on the european market. the law is similar to the regulations in force for new cars. the new regulation limits co2 emissions to an average of 175 grams of co2 per kilometre by 2017 and aims to limit it to 147 g/km by 2020. 177 amendments were tabled and 4 compromises were supported by the majority of political groups to confirm the will to achieve the 2020 target, adding an additional target for 2025, to achieve 105-120 gco2/km. i welcome the fact that it was adopted by a large majority, because we must bear in mind that this directive also makes it possible, in the second place, through the necessary investments, to reduce fuel consumption, to maintain a first-rate european production, to promote technological innovation while benefiting the environment. this legislation is therefore clearly beneficial both for consumers and for the european automobile industry.
in writing. i welcome the adoption of this new european co2 emission standard for light commercial vehicles. they will have to be reduced to 147 gr/co2/km by 2020, compared to 203 gr/co2/km today. this is largely achievable for european manufacturers, who have significantly improved their energy performance year after year, thanks to their r&d efforts and the stimulating legislative framework put in place by parliament. the system also gives them room for manoeuvre, since this is the average emission limit per manufacturer. this will enable manufacturers to produce enough low-emission models to strike the right balance with the most polluting vehicles on the market. this flexible system will also make it possible to offer a diversified range to customers who want products tailored to their needs. it is therefore in the interests of manufacturers, consumers and citizens that the council should follow the reasonable position of our assembly, in line with our ambitious objectives of combating pollution.

in writing. the lisbon treaty gave the european commission the power to adopt delegated acts, allowing for amendments to non-essential elements of legislative acts, and implementing acts. in order to ensure the consistency of european legislation, the legislative act opening and providing for the administration of certain community tariff quotas for certain meat and cereal products should be adapted accordingly. i agree with this report that it is essential, however, that the european parliament be properly involved in the preparation and implementation of these delegated acts.
in writing. i voted in favour of this text, which aims to bring this regulation into line with the european treaties. the midi-pyrénées and particularly the gers are areas where poultry production represents a significant part of the economy. the text will make it possible to streamline the european union's action in this area, which i welcome.
in writing. the commission proposal aims to align council regulation (ec) no 774/94 opening and providing for the administration of certain community tariff quotas for certain meat and cereals with articles 290 and 291 of the treaty on the functioning of the european union. under that regulation, some important changes concern the involvement of the european parliament in the preparation and implementation of delegated acts, the limitation of the delegation of power to five years, the extension of the time limit for objecting to a draft delegated act from two to four months and, finally, the modification of the application of the written procedure.
in writing. the commission proposal aims to adapt the regulation governing the import of meat and cereals in accordance with the treaties. the commission shall be granted the capacity to act by means of delegated acts in managing the opening and the manner of management of the quotas, following an agreement with a third country or countries. the fixing of import quotas implies the fixing of the volumes of products authorized for importation into the community market. the commission has consistently shown that it intends to liberalize trade completely and to remove the substance of customs instruments of trade regulation, such as tariff quotas. the report aims to ensure the involvement of parliament in the preparation and implementation of those delegated acts. you have no ambition. it cannot conceal its substance: the commission is increasing its unchecked appropriation of a people's right to rule. i vote against it.
in writing. i voted in favour of this report on the community tariff quotas for high-quality beef, pigmeat, poultrymeat, wheat (wheat and meslin) and soot, render and other residues. the report aims to bring the provisions of the regulation on the opening and administration of certain community tariff quotas for these products into line with the treaty of lisbon. behind this european jargon are in fact procedures to frame the exercise of the implementing powers conferred on the european commission. the report thus provides that the commission has the possibility to legislate by means of delegated acts and implementing acts in this regulation. it also recalled that the european parliament must be duly involved in the preparation and implementation of delegated acts. the delegation of power shall be tacitly extended for periods of an identical duration, for a period of five years.

in writing. flavoured wine products are a category of drinks including sangria or vermouth. the main purpose of this text, which is of a technical nature, is to update the rules applicable to aromatised wine products and bring them into line with the treaty of lisbon adopted in 2009. i voted in favour of this report.
in writing. i voted for the bartolozzi report on aromatised wine products to improve transparency on geographical indications.
in writing. this text improves the traceability of european aromatised wine drinks. by giving new contexts and origins to these products, it protects designations of origin and supports european winegrowers. but it is also about restoring consumer confidence by opting for more transparency. the efforts to clarify the manufacturing methods are particularly noteworthy.
in writing. i voted in favour of this text, which aims to simplify and clarify the definition, designation, presentation and labelling of aromatised wine products and the protection of their geographical indications. as a member of parliament representing a constituency which includes the hills of languedoc-roussillon, the south-west and bordeaux, this issue is particularly close to my heart. with this new text, a policy of quality and clarity will be put in place for the consumer, which i welcome.
in writing. this report supports new, looser regulations for flavoured wine products. this proposal further aggravates the 1991 regulation which granted aromatised alcoholic preparations the qualification of 'wine product', in line with the global trade liberalisation which affected the international wine organisation. historically, however, wine could be called only the product of the alcoholic fermentation of the grapes. by giving the term 'vinicole' to all kinds of products that have nothing to do with wine, this 'simplification' marked a regression for the protection of wine. the proposed european regulation makes this trivialization even worse. it extends to aromatised, sweetened and coloured products the qualifications which were hitherto reserved for wine alone, such as the indication of the grape variety or the geographical origin. this trend, which favours standardised industrial alcoholic products, will be to the detriment of quality wine producers, who are gradually losing their specific protections. this is very bad news for the future and diversity of european wines. and it is a further sign of the lack of taste of the arrogant and vulgar technostructure which is inventing such a crime against european civilization. i vote against it.
in writing. the report aims to relax the rules on aromatised wine products . in practice, it allows products flavoured, coloured or sweetened to benefit from qualifications previously reserved for wines only. these products will thus be able to boast a specific grape variety or geographical origin. traditional wines are losing these distinctive signs, creating confusion which is detrimental to these products which are a valuable piece of know-how which we must preserve. the consumer is also penalized because it will be more difficult for him to distinguish a simple flavoured product from a real wine. i therefore resolutely opposed this report.
in writing. i abstained on the report on the proposal for a regulation on the definition, designation, presentation, labelling and protection of geographical indications of aromatised wine products. the proposal for a regulation is part of the reform of the wine sector policy in the european union in the context of simplification of the cap. supporting transparency, providing guarantees on these names and ensuring consumer protection and information seem to me to be clearly sustainable objectives. it is probably necessary to provide information on the composition of these products, their geographical origin and their origin, and thus to avoid misleading names. but aligning these protections with those offered to quality wines, and ultimately losing the specific protection that existed for these wines, puts aromatised and often industrial wine products on the same level as traditional quality wine and can therefore be dangerous for traditional products and may cause more confusion for the consumer than real transparency.
in writing. i welcome the revision of the aromatised wine regulation to clarify the existing rules. on the one hand, parliament updates the many existing trade names to ensure better visibility for consumers. the text also relaxed the rules on the composition of these specific drinks, while strengthening health guarantees. this revision will not upset the major european producers and thus responds to their wish to modernise, without revolutionizing, a fair but obsolete legislative framework.
in writing. carbon capture and storage (ccs) is a promising technology that could reduce co2 emissions in the atmosphere in the future. it therefore needs political and possibly financial support to determine as soon as possible whether it is a viable technology in the long term and, if so, to enable the actors to invest. this own-initiative report supports innovation and the fight against climate change. that is why i voted for this one.
in writing. carbon capture and storage technology is by no means a panacea. however, there is still a long way to go in the fight against climate change. 2013 was another record-breaking year of warm weather, and the scenarios outlined by all the experts are truly chilling! the european union must therefore be the leader in cutting-edge technologies in this field. to do this, it must initiate, support and monitor new co2 capture and storage projects. however, companies receiving such support cannot be exempted from liability in the event of a leak. it is a win-win approach that is worth pursuing and one that i have stood up for.
in writing. i voted for the report on carbon capture and storage. this is a rather sensitive subject in the committee on petitions, where i have received petitions against this type of project which may pose a risk in the event of a change in the nature of the soil or an earthquake. france must continue to invest in research and security around these types of projects to remain at the forefront of this field.
in writing. by voting for this text, meps wanted to encourage the development of technologies for carbon capture and storage. this technology would enable us to achieve significant reductions in co2 emissions and bring us closer to our environmental objectives. therefore, it is particularly relevant to look more seriously at how to attract investment to enable the deployment of carbon capture and storage.
in writing. under its horizon 2020 strategy, the eu has set itself the ambition of reducing its greenhouse gas emissions by at least 20% by 2020. to achieve this, lifestyles will have to change. innovative technologies will also be needed to combine, where possible, the optimal use of energy with respect for our environmental commitments. in close cooperation with industry and member states, the eu supports demonstration projects and the development of carbon capture and storage (ccs). the heads of state and government have committed to setting up 12 demonstration plants by 2015. but none of these plants has yet been built and the delay in launching demonstration projects at european level may jeopardise the objectives set. we must not lose sight of this objective, which, in addition to reducing greenhouse gases, will be a source of growth and employment for europe.
in writing. i voted in favour of this report to put forward carbon capture and storage technologies. this proposal guarantees the application of technology which has a vital role to play in combating the threat of global warming and at a time when environmental issues remain a concern for many citizens, i welcome the adoption of such measures.
in writing. i voted in favour of this text, which aims to support the development of carbon capture and storage (ccs) technologies in europe and their role in the fight against climate change. for example, carbon dioxide emitted by highly emitting facilities, such as fossil fuel power stations, would be captured and stored underground. co2 could also be used as a raw material in industrial processes. all solutions to mitigate the effects of climate change are worth trying. the commission will continue to monitor the implementation of the cfp, in particular by ensuring that the cfp is properly managed and implemented. as such, they need to be mentioned in the 2030 climate and energy package.
in writing. i voted in favour of this report, which highlights the glaring lack of public and private investment in carbon capture and storage (ccs) technologies. despite all the efforts, carbon capture and storage technologies have still not taken off in europe. once again, the eu is lagging behind! the ccs is an essential tool for achieving a competitive low-carbon economy at low cost. clearly, investment in these technologies needs to be encouraged and attracted, and the public sector needs to play its part. ccs technologies are not 'competing' with renewable energy, but are an alternative technology, indispensable in certain industrial sectors that emit high levels of co2. faced with such potential, europe cannot afford to remain the last pupil in the class!
in writing. it is clear that since its adoption in 2009, the carbon capture and storage (ccs) directive has not had the desired effect: to date, no pilot plants have yet been set up. it was therefore essential that parliament should take stock of the application - or more precisely the non-application - of this directive and of the improvements needed to ensure that the development of this technology was both effective and supervised. 'effective' because it is important that europe can have low carbon electricity as ccs could be the only way to achieve european targets for reducing greenhouse gases from industrial sources. 'encadrated' as it is equally important to clarify that ccs should not be considered as an alternative to renewable energy; if the csc technology is to benefit from the financial resources necessary for its use, it must not become a blank check for polluters. the commission is also proposing to extend the scope of the directive to include the use of the term 'competent authority' to cover all the activities of the european union. i therefore decided to support this report, which, at the end of the negotiations, was a satisfactory balance.
in writing. this text is an example of the ecological inconsistency of european technocracy. he contradicts himself when he says that support for carbon capture and storage (ccs) technologies must be based on carbon market mechanisms after pointing out its inefficiency. he is loyal to the eu's neoliberal austerity line. thus, member states should play the supporting role through public-private partnerships of private companies in the development of gas pipelines at european level. they should also bear part of the industrial risk associated with the co2 storage activity. finally, it is also fully in line with the eu's anti-poor policy. as the commission does not intend to take the money where it is, it is envisaged here to finance support for the csc through a new form of taxation of fossil fuels. the increase will again be high for households with modest energy and transportation expenditure constraints. this is without questioning the eu's real need for renewable energy, whereas funding renewable energy is more environmentally and socially efficient. i vote against it.
in writing. this own-initiative report supports the development of carbon capture and storage (ccs) technologies in the european union. unfortunately, the development of these technologies implies that this will probably come at the expense of low greenhouse gas emitting technologies, such as renewable energy, and will mainly benefit large industrial groups. the development of the csc therefore offers no real answers to the climate and energy problems, and implicitly supports the ultra-productivist methods of the most emitting industrialists. for all these reasons, i voted against this report.
in writing. the european parliament and the council adopted the carbon capture and storage directive in 2009, which provides a framework for the eu. however, due to the lack of funding for technological development, there were no projects under way in the eu. however, the issue of global warming has become a matter of life and death and this possibility of capture must be studied in order to limit it. in his draft the rapporteur focused on possible ways to advance the development of carbon capture and storage in the eu, in particular through financial and regulatory measures. he also stressed the role of the member states in this area in relation to transport, storage and responsibility for co2 emissions. renewable energy, energy efficiency and their financing should remain the main focus of eu climate legislation. carbon capture and storage should be considered as a transitional solution to reduce greenhouse gas emissions from industrial sources. i supported the adoption of this own-initiative report because i believe that no possibility should be ruled out.
in writing. as every year since the adoption of the 2009 co2 storage directive, our parliament adopted a report on progress made. i welcome the fact that the european framework for the development of carbon capture and storage technologies is bearing fruit. it is both a niche for innovation, r&d and employment, and an effective means of achieving our emissions reduction targets. we know that this strategy requires investment by the industrialists and therefore european and national incentives. our report thus recognises the crucial role of the member states, which must play their part in supporting the eu's ambitious approach and step up their efforts to use the available funding. it is clear that there are sources of carbon emissions that cannot be eliminated, in industry or transport. nevertheless, the regulations in place for carbon capture and storage are indispensable and complement the efforts for the development of alternative energies and fuels. the main challenge for the future is now to accelerate research to improve the transport and geological storage of carbon that is captured at source and in the atmosphere.

in writing. 'online healthcare', as defined by the european commission, is the use of information and communication technologies in the interaction between patients and healthcare providers, the transmission of data between institutions, or the communication between patients and/or healthcare professionals. e-health can be a real breakthrough for people in sparsely populated, remote and/or isolated areas who have difficulty accessing healthcare. this text was therefore a real opportunity to open up these medical deserts and improve the quality and efficiency of healthcare in europe. unfortunately, by leaving the area of ehealth in the hands of the private sector, this text risks leading to a disengagement of public policies that would be very detrimental to citizens. i therefore opposed the report.

in writing. following the horse meat scandal which occurred almost a year ago in my own region of south-west france, i am pleased that our parliament has been able to draw up an own-initiative report on food crises and fraud in the food chain and on the means of combating these practices. the socialists supported the general approach of mrs de lange's report. with my colleague gilles pargneau, the s&d group's fictitious rapporteur, we have passed amendments calling for the creation of an anti-food fraud network to prevent crises and improve consumer information. thanks to our efforts, parliament is now demanding that the commission make it compulsory to label all meat with the indication of origin. it also called on the commission, in particular, to act as soon as possible by making legislative proposals to extend the mandatory labelling of the indication of origin for ingredients.

in writing. if the horse meat case has any merit, it is that it has highlighted the existence of flaws in a complex european agri-food production system that directly affects the health of our consumers, all over europe. in supporting this own-initiative report, i therefore call for the legislative framework for the european agri-food system to be strengthened, in particular by requiring that the origin labelling of meat used in cooked dishes be made compulsory. in addition, cases of fraud should be severely punished, including by imposing a fine equivalent to twice the profit sought by the fraudsters and by increasing penalties in cases where the victims are infants or vulnerable persons.
in writing. alarmed by the succession of food scandals that made headlines last year, the european parliament has sent a roadmap to the european commission and the member states to ensure that such practices do not happen again. while the eu is working to improve food security through a series of measures that are sometimes perceived as burdensome by citizens and that have never been more secure, these frauds and manipulations have largely contributed to discrediting european action and undermining consumer confidence. i therefore call on the commission and the national authorities to strengthen checks and to increase sanctions against fraudsters who do not hesitate to speculate on the health of citizens. finally, i would urge the commission to make proposals as soon as possible on the labelling of the origin of meat in prepared dishes, which are sometimes of poor quality, so that the citizen is fully informed of the quality of the products he consumes. let us not allow the idea to spread that the eu is just an uncontrolled market, left in the hands of a handful of irresponsible and fraudulent people.

in writing. the horse meat scandal last year exposed all the flaws in the agri-food chain. this type of deception, which is far from an isolated case, requires a reinforcement of the traceability system at european level. first, there must be strict sanctions against fraudsters. secondly, there is a need to increase the number of checks and inspections by national and european authorities at all stages of production, to coordinate the alert mechanisms better and finally to introduce mandatory and precise labelling of the origin of meat and fish in prepared dishes. beyond the fraud, it is the whole food trading system that seems to be the source of these unacceptable deviations. it is no longer a question of producing to sell, but of buying cheaply to sell and making the most profit, which is no more and no less than financial speculation in agri-food products. it is essential to return to a more transparent, clearer and more ethical system with fewer intermediaries and which values local production and short circuits.

in writing. following the horse meat scandal, the own-initiative report by mr de lange deals with ways of combating fraud in the food chain. food fraud affects a wide range of products including meat, fish, organic food, olive oil, milk and cereals. food fraud is becoming common. member states must take the necessary and substantial measures to implement effective controls in the food chain and to apply appropriate penalties in order to ensure public health and restore consumer confidence. this report suggests regulatory action. on the one hand by proposing a harmonisation of the definition of food fraud, and on the other hand by listing what contributes to this fraud. it encourages improved cooperation, proposes the introduction of a european revision regulation on labelling and the establishment of an electronic system for the rapid exchange of information to deal with cases of fraud. i welcome the adoption of this text which stresses the need for swift and more stringent action.
in writing. i voted in favour of this report on fraud in the food chain. unfortunately, in recent years there has been an increase in fraud in the food chain (so-called organic eggs, horse meat) and it is not surprising that one in three consumers no longer trusts the information mentioned on food labels. the report proposes several ways of restoring european consumers' confidence: - to find a harmonised european definition of food fraud; - to strengthen the role and resources of the european food and veterinary office in detecting food fraud cases; - to encourage member states to cooperate more through europol in cross-border food fraud investigations; - to increase penalties to at least double the economic gains sought by food fraud. although the eu is often called into question, in this case the responsibility for combating fraud in this area lies much more with the member states; the report therefore essentially encourages the states to act by giving them a european framework.
in writing. following the horse meat scandal in early 2013, the european parliament launched a work to analyse fraud in the food chain and to define measures to be taken to combat such abuses. the report i voted for today contains a range of concrete proposals, including a harmonised definition of food fraud, a revision of labelling rules, stronger penalties, the creation of an anti-food fraud network, the extension of the scope of the european rapid alert system for food and feed. socialist amendments, which i supported, also called for the obligation to indicate the origin of meat in prepared dishes, which is a real step forward, in line with the need to give a european response to this phenomenon of food fraud. we have thus succeeded, and i welcome this, in the report calling for the adoption of a legislative proposal extending the obligation to indicate the origin of meat in prepared dishes. i will be particularly careful to ensure that this text guarantees consumer information on the place of birth, rearing and slaughter of the animal, because this proposal will make all processors responsible.
in writing. the fight against food fraud is a relatively new item on the eu agenda and i welcome that it has become a priority. the european citizens would not understand that we should stand by while scandals have been unleashed in recent years, whether it be the issue of horse meat, transport and storage conditions or labelling. europe has the strictest health standards in the world, ensuring food safety throughout the internal market. it is therefore essential to guarantee quality throughout the food chain, from the field to the plate. i naturally supported the call on the commission to launch a comprehensive strategy to strengthen consumer confidence and improve the functioning of the food chain, while ensuring the stability of agricultural prices, without which the practices of impunity of the past will not be eradicated. the agri-food sector is one of the main industries in europe and we cannot afford to ignore significant progress in the fight against fraud. finally, i believe that our approach is inseparable from the strengthening of efforts to combat food waste, which is an equally unacceptable scandal.

in writing. the european union must have the means to combat undeclared work and the shadow economy, which represents a shortfall of 18.8% of its gdp. the creation of european standards for labour inspection goes hand in hand with the deepening of the common market, as does the creation of a european social security card covering all categories of workers. more effective and rigorous labour inspections and closer cooperation between national authorities would also help to improve working conditions in europe. in this respect, social dumping must be combated, particularly fraud in the case of secondment. the european union will therefore have to rethink its legislation on posted workers, some 1.5 million of whom are women. the 1996 directive is not sufficiently protective and does not define precisely the criteria for distinguishing between genuine secondment and fraud. it will therefore need to be reformed to put an end to the fiscal and social dumping practices within the eu which are destabilising large parts of our economy.

in writing. i voted against the report on financial participation by employees in company results because, in my view, it is not, as the report says, a good way to participate in so-called smart, sustainable and inclusive growth. employee shareholding, although it can bring profits when there are some (and in the period of crisis we are going through, nothing is less certain), above all places significant risks on employees since it puts them in a position that can be doubly precarious with the risk of losing both their job (and therefore their income) and the capital invested in the company. this also creates the illusion among workers that by participating in the results of their enterprise they have some power of decision in the strategies of the enterprise. we know what it's like in big business. and in fact, it only serves to mask the refusal to raise wages. i have been campaigning for many years in favour of the social and solidarity-based economy, and i would rather allow workers to take back their businesses through democratic means and support initiatives for other forms of ownership and employee participation than support such a mirror to the hips.

madam president, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, i welcome the agreement reached on this crucial issue for growth and employment, on which we have been working for several years, and i would like to congratulate the rapporteur on his excellent work. public procurement, by virtue of its importance in the economy, is essential to fostering quality employment and environmental responsibility while providing quality services and products to citizens. these texts meet this challenge, in particular because we have finally abandoned the simplistic logic of the least-good, leaving the public authorities the possibility of choosing the best economic offer on the basis of qualitative, social and environmental criteria and taking into account the constraints faced by smes in accessing public contracts. i also expect the authorities of the member states to play their part in controlling the drift towards subcontracting and social dumping, since they will now have the legal tools to do so. finally, i regret that we have not been able to secure the reciprocity clause in both texts and i expect the commission to play its full part so that the union will no longer be naive and will no longer be the only one to set an example.

madam president, even if the text raises many differences among the members of this house and also among the member states, the commission's initiative has the merit of raising certain questions which seem to me to be essential on the balance of international trade, cohesion and the unity which europe wants and can display towards its partners. we have heard many criticisms, still today in the debates, particularly on its legitimacy and purpose, but it seems essential to recall that the consultations that have been carried out have shown that a majority of respondents share the commission's view on the degrees of openness and lack of reciprocity and, more specifically, that 75% of the representatives of the business world are in favour of union action through a legislative instrument. it is not a protectionist instrument to preserve our markets, as some would like to make it out to be, but a response to the real problem, namely that 50% of public contracts in the world are now closed to european companies because of protectionist measures. it is therefore legitimate to try to achieve real transparency and equal treatment among our partners and to consider the tools to achieve this. with this regulation we are simply giving ourselves the means to act. we are sending a clear message to our partners that the same rights will in future mean the same obligations. i would like to thank and congratulate mr caspary, who has done an excellent job of reconciling all the points of view on this text. i therefore call on the council to listen to the voice of the citizens.
in writing. the european commission is finally responding to the criticism, repeatedly voiced, that the european union opens up its public procurement much more than its other trading partners. it has long thought that the public procurement agreement, a recently revised instrument of the world trade organization, could be sufficient to defend us. but this is not the case, and this reciprocity instrument was designed not only to better defend european public procurement against unfair foreign offers, but also to be able to investigate and impose sanctions on countries that do not apply reciprocal opening conditions. the european commission will also have the right, on its own initiative or on request, to investigate restrictive procurement practices applied by third countries. this instrument is absolutely necessary in the present context and i hope that the work on the text can be completed quickly so that the regulation can enter into force as soon as possible.
madam president, commissioner, may i offer you my best wishes, including the hope of being able to taste honey as it is produced by our bees and distributed by our beekeepers. the revision of the honey directive is symptomatic of the errors of judgment which may sometimes be made by elected officials. some of my colleagues, with good intentions, believe that they can consider pollen as an ingredient in honey, even though nature intended pollen to be a natural constituent of honey. does anyone have any questions about the egg? is the question raised whether the egg yolk is an ingredient or a natural component of the egg? pollen is naturally present in honey, regardless of whether the honey is extracted by the beekeeper or not. in no case do beekeepers intentionally add pollen to honey. yet some of my colleagues want to go against nature and deny this natural reality. i understand, of course, the important questions that arise behind this question. yes, i think consumers should be informed about the presence of trace amounts of gmos in food products and i fully support the rule that any ingredient containing at least 0.9% gmos is or should be labelled as such. but we're talking about ingredients here, not natural constituents like pollen. this rule does not and cannot apply to pollen or, even less so, to honey. i can tell you, ladies and gentlemen, that the beekeepers in my region, which is a beekeeping region, are very happy that this rule does not apply to honey. indeed, as my colleague mr davis has said, bees sometimes forage tens of kilometres from their hive in fields of all kinds and have no gps or high-tech system to avoid contact with gmos. i am not kidding, but let us get back to reality, it would be totally irresponsible to require all beekeepers to test every single pot of honey to make sure that the bees have not been in contact with gmos.
madam president, as i listen to this debate, i think it is really time to save the honey product because, under very technical circumstances, the vote tomorrow will be a crucial vote for the future of a beekeeping industry which is already unfortunately weakened by the fate of our bees. to consider pollen as an ingredient in honey is a scientific aberration. honey is present in the hive as a finished product. pollen is just one natural component. if honey were to be considered as being made up of ingredients, then it would be easy to manipulate it, to alter it. an ingredient can, by definition, be added, removed or altered. this would open the door to our markets for honey produced by industrial techniques, of which china, for example, is a major producer. has the commission considered the considerable economic burden that would be imposed on our beekeepers, who are often small producers, and who would then be subject to disproportionate labelling requirements? they would be forced to perform extremely expensive tests. the consumer's demand for information is, of course, legitimate, but it does not justify our taking the beekeeping industry hostage in the general debate on gm crops. in the name of a precautionary principle taken to its extreme, a whole sector is being murdered. pollen is just one of the ingredients in honey. to say otherwise is a threat to this product and is consumer misinformation. let's not get this wrong, the survival of our beekeepers depends on it. that is why i support the commission's proposal.
in writing. i consider pollen to be a constituent of honey and not an ingredient. the 'ingredient' approach would require gmo labelling for honey containing only a few grains, and this would be done on a random basis. this allows lots to be declared positive in certain countries that do not grow gmos. remember that, because of the biology of bees, their prey distance varies constantly depending on the food sources present, up to 13 km. considering pollen as an ingredient, with only 9 grains out of a total of 1000 grains of maize pollen, the presence of gmo pollen should be indicated, whereas this presence reduced to total pollen would only be 0.009% (i.e. 100 times less than the community labelling threshold for random presence set at 0.9%). this would have a devastating impact on the image of honey and on the future of the european beekeeping industry, which is already suffering from competition from foreign honey of lower quality and is expected to bear exorbitant analytical costs despite analytical uncertainties. if honey is no longer considered as a whole product but as a composite of ingredients, then it can be filtered, cut with other products, ultra-filtered or pasteurized.
in writing. parliament is expected to turn by beekeepers on this vote on the honey directive. will we create a legislative inflation that will upset the whole industry, or, on the contrary, will we want to protect ancestral know-how and many jobs? i would of course urge you to choose the second option and not to support an unfair and counterproductive legislative revolution. giving honey an ingredient status would force beekeepers to test all their lots and would lead to disproportionate or difficult to overcome production costs. the benefit to the consumer would also be very limited (obligatory labelling linked to ingredient status), compared with the new costs imposed on producers. pollen is a tiny component of honey and therefore does not deserve all this regulatory attention. let us show that the eu knows how to work with good sense and that the regulatory obsession is not as prevalent as eurosceptics would have us believe.
the main issue in the regulation we have been working on is to regulate the production of community statistics on trade in goods between member states. the regulation determines the powers of the commission and lays down the appropriate procedure to enable it to adopt measures under its powers. we have agreed to guarantee the efficient and free exchange of statistical data by establishing a coherent system. however, as regards the exchange of confidential data, the rapporteur has maintained in his text the idea of absolute confidentiality, which implies that no confidential data should be used for other purposes. while this principle may seem legitimate, i believe it is also extremely important not to exclude the existence of exceptional cases, otherwise we will be proposing legislation that is too manic and too rigid. these exceptions would allow the disclosure of such confidential information under certain conditions. this idea is not disconnected from the other texts since article 20 of regulation 223/2009 itself specifies that, in certain exceptional cases, statistical data may be disseminated and used for other purposes. this idea is not without its usefulness. this data could be used for tax purposes, which would be a first step towards tax harmonisation at european level. as you can see, these technical arguments are largely political. i wonder today why the rapporteur is reluctant to introduce this principle of openness into his text, despite our many attempts to reach a compromise. i have wanted to work in good faith with the rapporteur on this matter and i regret that i was not able to exchange as much information as was necessary. i am, of course, open to a compromise until the time of the vote, but i am not in a position to support the text as it stands.

in writing. the european parliament delivered its opinion on wednesday 15 january on the widespread use of smart tachographs. these devices which record information on the journeys of heavy goods vehicles are used to monitor compliance with labour law by transport companies which, as we know, use methods which are unworthy of their employees. i voted for the general use of this tool, which is indispensable in the fight against the excessive abuses of road transport companies, which are by their nature difficult to control, but let us be vigilant. such a tool collects a great deal of data, and should not be used against employees. and let us not be delusional, if this is a positive step towards more control of existing legislation that must be respected, it is not enough. to prevent social dumping on the road, the european union must at least have legislation to prohibit cabotage and better coordinated social legislation in the interests of employees, which means taking competition out of the centre of its actions.
in writing. the purpose of this proposal for a directive is to lay down rules on the award of works or service concession contracts. today, concessions are not subject to a clear legislative framework at european level, unlike public procurement. it is therefore necessary to clarify the legal framework and to establish clear and effective rules. i believe that the agreement before us is a balanced compromise, given the difficulties of the file, and i have voted in favour of it and i congratulate my colleague, the rapporteur, mr philippe juvin, who has done a great deal of work.

in writing. the proposal for a directive published by the commission on 20 december 2011, for which i am the rapporteur in the european parliament, aims to define rules for the award of works or service concession contracts. the text adopted on 15 january 2014 in plenary following the agreement reached in the trilogue last july between the three institutions (european parliament, european commission and council) after almost two years of work is a major step forward in strengthening the internal market. it creates a new legal framework which is robust, clear, pragmatic and adapted to the specific nature of the concession. it strikes the right balance between the need for flexibility and leeway for public authorities on the one hand and the need for transparency and non-discrimination for economic operators on the other. the original legislative proposal of the european commission has been substantially rewritten, in particular to clarify the concept of concession and to introduce the necessary flexibility in the negotiation procedure. the final text preserves the free administration of the public authorities (the right to choose the mode of management of their public works and services which they consider most appropriate: concession, management, inter-municipal cooperation, etc.) and constitutes a balanced compromise.
in writing. i voted in favour of this report on the concession award directive in conjunction with the other two items on the agenda for this plenary on public procurement. as a green/efa group we had initially voted against in the imco commission but the negotiations during the trilogue had resulted in the removal of public water services from the directive, which was one of the key points for us. we were very much afraid that this would lead to privatisation of the water sector, which we are firmly opposed to. i am pleased that the mobilisation of civil society at european level, with the european citizens' initiative on water, has borne fruit and shown that convergent actions inside and outside parliament can contribute to real policy changes that impact on citizens' daily lives. in the field of public-public cooperation, a satisfactory solution has also been found with a fairly broad definition of this concept, leaving sufficient room for manoeuvre for public authorities both horizontally and vertically.

in writing. concessions represent a significant part of the economic activity of the european union. until then, no text had been adapted to this specific case, leading to growing legal uncertainty and instability. the adoption of a directive explicitly mentioning the award of concession contracts was therefore a necessary step in order to make the european legal framework as transparent as possible. i am glad that i voted in favour of this report with a view to creating a directive on concession contracts. the directive will put an end to distortions of the single market such as favouritism and lack of transparency. every company will now be guaranteed fair access to the concession market. we will emerge from this crisis, which has been raging for years, with a more transparent, stable and secure european economy. this type of report enables us, step by step, to build a european union that lives up to its ambitions.
in writing. until now, there has been no european legislation on the award of concession contracts. the current situation is very heterogeneous: some member states fully regulate this form of public procurement (france in particular), while others have no rules at all - which can encourage an opaque use of public funds. in order to boost the european internal market and bring more transparency to this form of public procurement, the commission has proposed to establish a number of common rules for the award of concession contracts in europe. the final text, which was the result of long negotiations, seems to me to be balanced. i am pleased to see that it does not fall into the trap of over-regulation, but rather sets out general principles and a common definition of 'concession'. for all these reasons, i support it.
in writing. i abstained on this report. there was no legislative framework in france for 'public service delegations' which allow the authorities to transfer the management of a public service or public works to an undertaking. it is not necessary to mention the deviations in this sector where the lack of a legislative framework in this area gradually led to treating public service concessions as simple public contracts without taking into account the specific nature of this mode of public management. the report recalls that the authorities decide autonomously whether it is preferable for them alone to provide goods and services of general interest and that the concern to satisfy the needs of the population takes precedence over compliance with the internal market criteria. this report improves on the commission's original proposal but it is sometimes lacking in firmness and leaves a number of questions unresolved. the legislator has therefore not fully assumed his role, even if we stick to it within the framework of the current european treaties. this is a battle that will have to be fought further, particularly in the next european elections campaign.
in writing. the purpose of this proposal for a directive is to update the 2004 directive on the award of public contracts. the aim is to simplify and relax the existing rules, to improve the consideration of societal objectives (energy efficiency, social inclusion) and to reduce the structural disadvantages faced by smes in accessing public procurement. as with the concession dossier, i consider that the agreement reached in the trilogue with the council and the commission on this text is satisfactory, and i therefore voted in favour of the report presented by my colleague, mr marc tarabella.
in writing. i supported the adoption of this text on public procurement. i particularly welcome the freedom left to the public authorities to choose not only the lowest price offer but also the 'most economically advantageous offer'. this allows them to base their choice on social and environmental criteria. the responsibility of the subcontracting chain, which will make it possible to combat social dumping, is also a major step forward.
in writing. the adoption of this text is the culmination of successful negotiations to adapt european public procurement legislation to economic and social developments in recent years. the need to strike a balance between simplified rules and sound and efficient procedures was emphasised. i particularly encourage the use of the 'code of good practice facilitating access to public procurement for smes', which promotes the integration of smes into public procurement.
in writing. although the reform of public procurement, which represents 18% of european gdp, was one of the priorities of the single european act, nothing had been done for 10 years. public procurement is a real strategic lever for jobs and growth in europe. the updating of public procurement rules in europe is therefore a step in the right direction. the legislative package, which will enter into force in 2016, changes the award criteria for contracts. in future, it will favour the most economically advantageous offers over the lowest ones. this will make it possible to take greater account of social and environmental aspects in tendering procedures, as well as international agreements and collective agreements. for example, abnormally low tenders - because they are linked to breaches of social or environmental legislation - will be automatically excluded. the use of subcontractors should also be made more transparent. finally, access to public procurement for smes will be facilitated by the use of contract allocation and the reduction of administrative burdens.
in writing. i supported this report on the award of public contracts, which is the result of an agreement reached in a trilogue last july between the three institutions (european parliament, european commission, council). the text adopted revises the existing directive 2004/18/ec and allows for the modernisation and simplification of the rules in force in this area: strategic use of public procurement, facilitation of access to contracts for small and medium-sized enterprises, dematerialization of procedures, and increased quality and transparency of award procedures. this modernisation of the rules was expected; the european parliament had previously published an own-initiative report on this subject. the result is an excellent compromise.
