in writing. in this time of crisis, it is necessary to take all the measures in our power to enable our companies to remain competitive within the union. i therefore support the report on public procurement, which is aimed at simplifying the rules governing relations between public authorities and the economic sector. this will mean that smaller, but nevertheless vital players in our economy, such as smes, will no longer be disadvantaged by tedious bureaucracy and will be able to flourish. the directive proposes the creation of a european economic market which respects the social rights of citizens and is concerned about their environmental welfare. it is essential to ensure that our companies respect these rights. the question now is to choose the most appropriate offer, not necessarily the cheapest, which will allow the creation of a fair european market. i am glad that such a report has been adopted by the members of this house. i remain convinced that it is with this kind of initiative that we will succeed in building a stronger europe, capable of meeting the challenges of our time.
in writing. public procurement represents 18% of european gdp and is an important lever for achieving objectives such as sustainable development, inclusive growth, innovation and the development of smes. in the current economic climate, it is essential to allocate public money in the best possible way. that is the purpose of this reform, and i wholeheartedly support it. the most important point seems to me to be the replacement of the criterion of the lowest price in the award of public contracts by that of the 'most economically advantageous tender'. this will allow public authorities to place greater emphasis on quality, environmental and social aspects, while taking into account price and life cycle costs of supply. in future, quality will be at the heart of european public procurement, and i welcome this. the reform will also boost innovation, facilitate the participation of small firms in public procurement, combat abnormally low tenders, and provide for more stringent rules on subcontracting, thus combating social dumping and non-compliance with labour law. member states now have 24 months to transpose these new rules.
in writing. public authorities in europe spend the equivalent of 18% of gdp on infrastructure and public services. a fifth of this expenditure is made by inviting private companies to tender, under procedures known as 'public procurement' or 'concession contract'. in order to avoid any favouritism, unfair competition or patronage, i voted in favour of this major reform of the existing rules. thanks to the work of our assembly, the tendering procedures will be simplified. they will also make it possible to add ecological and social criteria so that the lowest cost candidate is no longer the only one to be favoured, and will promote access to public contracts for small and medium-sized enterprises.
in writing. i voted in favour of this very important text on the european union's trade policy and reciprocity in access to public procurement. it is a technical text but it is crucial for the health of the european economy. public procurement accounts for between 15 and 20% of the european union's economy and many companies - particularly french companies - are highly competitive in this sector. at present, european public procurement is very open, which means that foreign companies can come and compete directly with european companies on european soil. our main trading partners, the united states and japan, on the contrary, give preference to their national companies when awarding public contracts: 32 per cent of us public contracts are open to european companies and only 28 per cent in japan. the adoption of this text, which provides for reciprocity in public procurement, will therefore make european companies better able to fight foreign competition, which will be beneficial for our economy and for jobs in europe! i therefore supported this report when it was put to the vote.
in writing. i voted in favour of this report on public procurement. it is the result of a long struggle by the european parliament against the liberal approaches advocated by the commission and most of the member states in this field. so we were very careful. the report gives public authorities more leeway in public procurement by reinforcing the obligation to respect social standards in procurement procedures: award criteria will no longer be based solely on the lowest cost but may take account of social and environmental objectives. in addition, any company that has breached its obligations under social, environmental or labour law can now be automatically excluded and the possibility of promoting a principle of responsibility in the subcontracting chain has been introduced to ensure that all economic actors respect the rights of workers. finally, the report confirms the creation of a special regime for social services of general interest which will not be covered by these rules when they are organised on a non-profit-making basis. if not, they will be so only from a threshold of eur 1 million.
in writing. i welcome this vote, which endorses a thorough modernisation of public procurement in the european union, a sector which represents 19% of european gdp. thanks to the hard work of the european socialists, the agreement reached in these legislation, which are crucial for growth and employment, brings a major change: the choice of the contracting authority will be based on the most economically advantageous tender, and no longer on the sole basis of the lowest price. the difference is fundamental: social and environmental criteria will therefore be taken into account, as will sustainability. these provisions are also extended to the subcontracting chain, the regulation of which is included in a european text for the first time, in particular to combat social dumping. these texts will make public spending more efficient while simplifying procedures for smes and their access to markets. as for local authorities, their autonomy of choice is reinforced by legal clarification between public procurement and concessions, and by the exclusion of 'public-public' cooperation and certain sectors for concessions, such as water, transport, energy, civil protection, or emergency services.

in writing. i voted in favour of this report on public procurement in the water, energy, transport and postal services sectors. like the more general report on public procurement, it is the result of a long struggle by the european parliament against the liberal drift of the commission and some member states. the report gives public authorities more room for manoeuvre by reinforcing the obligation to respect social standards in procurement procedures. and we know that there are deviations in this area, particularly in france, where the public authorities have found themselves without recourse to the large companies in the sector. in addition, social and environmental objectives will be part of the award criteria, not just the lowest cost. the principle of responsibility in the subcontracting chain is introduced. the creation of a special scheme for social services of general interest, setting a threshold of eur 1 million and excluding non-profit-making from the criteria, is confirmed. the report is imperfect, does not go far enough, but does present some advances compared to the current texts. it is part of the battles fought, in particular, within the framework of the intergroup on public services, of which i am vice-president with the ssig collective.

in writing. this text reflects the european union's efforts to open up public procurement to its companies in third countries. the european union is indeed committed to increasing trade. the text thus aims to encourage third countries to open up their markets by regulating the access of foreign products and services to european public procurement. in order to continue these negotiations, it seems particularly reasonable to ensure that the principle of uniformity of the common commercial policy is preserved by including the award of contracts.
in writing. by voting on access of goods and services to the public procurement market, parliament sent a strong message to the rest of the world about the principle of reciprocity in trade relations. at present, some public contracts in third countries are still not open to european companies and investments, whereas our markets are open to the rest of the world. the eu therefore decided to give itself the opportunity to react by closing its markets to companies from countries that do not play fairly in international competition. the decision to exclude companies from 'unfair' countries from european public procurement is taken by the commission. however, the national authorities of the 28 may, in the name of the principle of commercial reciprocity, request authorisation to exclude a particular country from their markets.

in writing. it is with a heavy heart that i abstained on mr caspary's report. in the present context, it seems logical to want to set up reciprocity instruments or to influence the opening up of public procurement in third countries whose companies already have access to public procurement in the european union. the problem is the general philosophy behind the text. while almost all countries in the world restrict access to public procurement, considering that taxpayers' money should primarily serve national objectives and benefit national companies, the european union has made the exact opposite choice. it has opted for total openness to global competition, to the extent that 90% of its public contracts are now fully competitive. the only real solution is the introduction of national rules of exclusivity and protection, which will encourage local businesses and employment. it is no longer possible, in a context of overtaxation which is legitimately being contested, to use taxpayers' money for the benefit of foreign companies in the name of your dogmas of competition and ultra-barterism. the legitimacy of taxation is first and foremost the legitimacy and acceptance by citizens of its use.
in writing. here is a report whose message and relevance can be welcomed. finally, the european parliament has taken a stand for a rebalanced globalisation to the benefit of the european union. it seems unthinkable to open our markets to firms from third countries which drive down prices and quality while our own firms remain at the doorstep of those countries which encourage their firms to engage in such practices. yet that is what the european union is doing and it has become intolerable! while public procurement in europe is 85% open, european companies have access to only one third of public procurement in the united states (32%) and only 28% in japan! let us not be the blessings of globalisation! i am glad that the eu is finally recognising this asymmetry and is restoring balance by advocating reciprocity in access to public procurement. a foreign company that submits an abnormally low bid may now be excluded if the reasons are not valid. it will also be possible to exclude tenders from countries whose public procurement remains closed to european companies. the eu will now be able to approach trade negotiations with ambition and realism.
in writing. i supported this report on reciprocity in access to public procurement. published in march 2012, this proposal for a regulation aims to restore fair competition between european companies and those from third countries in access to public contracts, by introducing a principle of reciprocal opening of public contracts and providing for the possibility of excluding tenders from foreign companies from countries that do not respect the principle of reciprocity. the text adopted provides for a number of conditions clarifying the application of this principle and takes account of the special case of the least developed countries. this text shows the european union's belated awareness of the need to act in this area: while nearly 85% of eu public procurement is open, some of our trading partners are resolutely closing access to their public procurement to european companies (in particular the united states, china and brazil). it was time for the eu to finally open its eyes and react.
in writing. we have adopted a key element of our commercial strategy, namely a reciprocity instrument in access to public procurement. this project was jointly promoted by commissioner michel barnier and his colleague karel de gucht and was able to benefit from the full support and commitment of all the meps of the french epp delegation. reciprocity must become the watchword of our trade policy. this is what nicolas sarkozy demanded when he was five years old, and it is a very important first step which has now been taken in this direction, despite the reluctance and reservations of those who see it as disguised protectionism. for my part, i welcome the fact that we are giving ourselves the means to be on equal footing in globalisation and to ensure reciprocal access for our european companies to public contracts in third countries.
in writing. the aim is to restrict access to eu public procurement by third countries that do not offer reciprocal access to their markets. but it goes to show that openness must be the rule. i don't think that's what you mean. in the context of the wto negotiations on the revision of the agreement on government procurement (gpa) and bilateral negotiations with third countries, the eu has advocated the opening up of public procurement at international level. public procurement is an important tool for development and national and popular sovereignty. developing countries in particular must be able to retain their freedom to reserve these markets for local operators, or to exclude certain key sectors from international competition. i am voting against this report.
in writing. the principle of reciprocity is a key principle for the proper conduct of economic relations between the european union and its international partners. however, the union's public procurement sector, which is ambitious in opening up to the rest of the world, is increasingly faced with restrictive practices by its major trading partners. i voted for the adoption of this report in the interests of improving trade relations between the union and these countries. we must protect our companies from unfair competition from the rest of the world. we do not see this as a measure of exacerbated protectionism but rather as a means of changing the union's relations with countries which have not, to date, shown any desire to enter into negotiations for an economic partnership. we need such an instrument so that our public market can develop in a global atmosphere conducive to its flourishing. i will always fight for a fairer trading relationship so that our economy can best serve our fellow citizens.
in writing. there are serious imbalances in access to public procurement between the eu and its trading partners: while 85% of eu public procurement contracts are already potentially open to international tenderers, this is the case for only 32% of public procurement contracts in the us and 28% in japan. the so-called 'reciprocity instrument' proposed by the commission is intended to remedy this situation - not to close our markets as some critics have claimed. this draft instrument would prevent non-european companies from being awarded public contracts in the eu if their country of origin does not itself offer this possibility to our companies. the proposed tool could only be used for contracts of at least €5 million, with the approval of the european commission, and the least developed countries would be excluded. the compromise reached seems satisfactory to me and i support it. i now call on the council to move constructively forward in the negotiations with parliament so that such a tool can be created as soon as possible.
in writing. i voted in favour of this draft regulation which allows european public procurement contracts to be closed to companies from countries which do not respect strict reciprocity. according to the commission, 85% of eu public contracts are already potentially open to international bidders, compared with only 32% of public contracts in the us and 28% in japan. without this text, the large multinationals in the newly industrialized countries would continue to benefit from the opening up of european markets without our companies being able to work in those countries. we had to create a legal framework which would enable the european union to respond to this unfair competition. this text is the logical continuation of our commitments to a more equitable globalisation in which europe defends its interests.
in writing. i voted against this legislative report on the access of products and services from third countries to the internal market of the union. the purpose of this headline is to restrict access to eu public contracts by third countries when they do not offer reciprocal access to their public contracts. in most cases, this is to strengthen the eu's position in opening up public procurement to so-called european companies and to clarify the rules governing access of third country companies and their products and services to eu public procurement. i am firmly opposed to this kind of blackmail by the eu on developing countries as if they were playing on equal terms. public procurement is an important tool for development in the countries of the south and these countries must be able to retain their freedom to reserve these contracts to local operators or to exclude certain key sectors from international competition. this report risks creating burdensome administrative procedures and even limiting the freedoms of local and regional authorities with the aim of facilitating the conquest of markets by predatory companies and, as a consequence, all-round social dumping.
in writing. i spoke today in favour of reciprocity in access to public procurement. i believe that this vote is a step towards the 'fair trade' which we european socialists advocate and oppose to general free trade and protectionism. reciprocity will now prevent non-european companies from bidding on european public contracts when their home country does not give european union companies full guarantees of reciprocal and fair access to its public contracts or does not respect international labour law. the correct application of the principle of reciprocity is also a strategic issue: european public contracts are open at 85%, while those of the united states are only open at 32%, those of japan at 28% and those of canada at 16%. our companies must be able to compete on equal terms with their competitors in third countries: this is a point we are negotiating very hard in the free trade agreements with these three countries! it is therefore an important weapon in the battle for employment which we are waging on all fronts.
in writing. the purpose of this legislation is to clarify the rules applicable to labelling in the event of the presence of gmos in honey. following a ruling by the court of justice of the european union, any package of honey containing traces of gmos had to be labelled as such, which implies unbearable costs for beekeepers because it requires tests on each jar of honey to detect the possible presence of gmos. indeed, a beekeeper can never be sure that his bees have not gone to gather in a gmo field. in view of this situation, the european commission recalled that pollen is not an ingredient but a natural constituent of honey and that the rules on labelling the presence of gmo ingredients in food should not be applied. the commission has therefore proposed a beneficial amendment to the legislation to ensure this clarification. i voted in favour of this report recalling the status of natural constituents of pollen in honey.
in writing. i voted for the amendments to the plenary to reaffirm the natural character of honey. a majority of the european parliament considered that pollen is a natural component of honey, not an ingredient. we want quality honey and proximity in the union. honey must remain a natural product. the mortality of bees, the quantity of pesticides or the quality of products, especially imported ones, require stringent criteria from the european union. the fight against genetically modified organisms (gmos) is also a priority. because of the concerns about the very nature of gmos, the best way to prevent their spread is to ban the production of such crops throughout the european continent.
in writing. by voting for this text, parliament is affirming that pollen is indeed a constituent of honey and not an ingredient that can be separated from it. to say otherwise would have had a detrimental impact on the beekeeping sector. in particular, it was allegedly subject to excessive labelling and testing requirements which would result in an increase in the price of honey, which would be detrimental to the consumer. a negative vote would also have ended the natural product status of honey and opened the door to the addition of artificial products.
in writing. i voted in favour of this text which aligns the commission's implementing powers with the provisions of the treaty on the functioning of the european union on clarification of the status of honey. in addition, it appears from this proposal that the commission would thus have the power to adopt delegated acts to lay down methods for verifying the compliance of honey with the provisions of directive 2001/110/ec.
in writing. i voted against the girling report amending council directive 2001/110 on honey because all the amendments relating to the classification of pollen as an ingredient from gm crops were rejected by a majority in the plenary vote. yes, pollen can be considered a natural component of honey and does not need to be indicated on the label. however, in the interests of transparency and consumer information, i think it is desirable to consider pollen as an ingredient when it comes from gm crops or when the honey has been imported from a gmo producing country. this approach, which respects eu legislation on gmo labelling, aims to address the concerns expressed by both consumers and beekeepers who are concerned about producing quality honey from eco-responsible agriculture. as this debate is not yet over, i hope that in the next stages of the negotiations we will be able to reach a consensus on the appropriate and applicable solutions to this problem.
in writing. i am pleased that parliament has confirmed the commission's position on the nature of pollen in honey, despite the decision of the court of justice of the eu. it is difficult for me to consider pollen as an external ingredient, since it is essential to the composition of honey. the commission has also proposed that the european parliament should be consulted on the proposal. while i understand that any trace of gmos above 0.9% found in an ingredient must be reported and labelled, this rule cannot apply to natural food constituents. how do you expect beekeepers to check jar by jar if their honey contains traces of gmos because a bee has been poaching in the wrong place? if legislation on gmos is to be made, it certainly does not have to be by penalising beekeepers who are only collateral victims of agricultural practices whose effects are not known. the number of beekeepers has fallen dramatically in recent years and we are buying more and more honey from countries whose production methods are far from as reliable as in europe. let's not burden them any more.
in writing. i voted in favour of the report by my colleague julie girling, who considers pollen to be a natural constituent of honey, not an ingredient. this will save honey producers from having to pay very high additional costs to check that each jar of honey does not contain pollen from gm plants. i therefore welcome the adoption of this report.
in writing. we have taken decisions on two dossiers related to the question of gmos. i first supported the report clarifying the legal status of pollen, particularly in relation to labelling in the event of traces of gmos in honey. i felt that the obligation to indicate the presence of traces of gmos, if such presence were to be found, would entail too high a cost for our beekeepers. i think that the consumer should be informed of the presence of traces of gmos in food products, but i think that pollen is a component of honey and not an ingredient. penalising our companies and beekeepers for traces of gmos that are caused by the fact that bees sometimes forage for gmos in fields several kilometres from their hives would have been an inadequate and costly administrative burden. on another report, however, i opposed the planting of the genetically modified maize pioneer tc 1507, given the lack of scientific evaluation of the possible environmental risks of this gmo which persist.
in writing. i call for a ban on the open-field cultivation of gmos. without going back to that objective, the report proposes to define pollen as an ingredient in honey, so that labelling of genetically modified pollen would be compulsory. this is a minimum of legitimate consumer protection. but the amendments have stripped the text of its substance, namely consumer protection in relation to gmos, so i voted against.
in writing. i voted against the idea of considering pollen as a mere ingredient of honey and not as a natural constituent of the product. this technical detail hides a much more political issue: defining pollen as an ingredient could open the way to dubious honey recipes (with mixtures or pollen substitutions). in addition, these changes involved a complete overhaul of the labelling system for jars and gmo tests on honey. the economic consequences would have been disastrous for most beekeepers. the use of this 'honey directive' by environmentalists in the name of the principle of excessive precaution put the whole beekeeping industry at risk.
in writing. bees have no borders, so pollen can come from any crop that is part of their habitat. the question is whether when honey contains pollen from gm crops, it should be reported. the commission and the rapporteur replied that pollen would be a natural constituent. i said, as my colleagues have said, that it is an ingredient. the whole nuance is in the labelling obligation. if the commission's proposal is accepted, the labelling obligation would only take effect from a threshold of 0.9%. however, the concentration is always less than 0.5%, so the proportion of gmos will never reach this legal threshold and will therefore never be reported. on the other hand, if pollen is considered to be an ingredient, it must be declared, whether the gmo is all or part of it, even if it is only a small part. i think that the freedom of information of consumers must be guaranteed. i regret that the majority of members do not see it that way, and that leaves the door open to abuse, favouring imported honey whose composition is not always known, as opposed to beekeepers who try to operate in a transparent way.
in writing. in 2001, the court of justice of the european union ruled that pollen is an ingredient and required the labelling of honey containing gm pollen. in 2012, the commission presented a revision of the so-called community honey legislation, and proposed that pollen be considered as a natural constituent of honey and not as an ingredient, thus circumventing the cjeu judgment. a very large majority in the european parliament (right-wing, pro-sovereignty, social democrats and liberals) considered that pollen is a natural constituent. i regret that it has thus rejected the mandatory labelling of honey containing gm pollen, referring this provision to the legislation on the labelling of gmos. this vote deprives beekeepers of protection against gmos, believing that beekeeping is no longer a problem for gm producers. the beekeepers and consumers are the winners of this revision. the activity of beekeepers is threatened because there is a suspicion of gmo contamination, since the consumer cannot be informed of the presence of gmos. the vote on l. 1507 maize also shows the inconsistency of meps on gmos.
in writing. determining whether flower pollen should be designated as an ingredient or a natural constituent of honey has many regulatory implications. if pollen is considered to be a natural constituent, no labelling is necessary; if, on the other hand, it is considered to be an ingredient, then beekeepers may, under certain conditions, be required to label their honey to inform the consumer about the presence of gmos in their product. my position, like that of the french socialists, has always been very clear: pollen is a natural constituent of honey but in the exceptional case where a honey contains pollen from gm crops, this pollen can be considered an ingredient under european legislation on the labelling of gmos. i regret the outcome of the vote in favour of the commission's proposal in the european parliament today. this is like hiding the presence of gmos from consumers! our approach would have supported all producers who are trying to bring to the market quality, non-gmo honey that meets consumer demand. but the fight is not over!
in writing. the hercule iii programme is designed to promote anti-fraud activities, in particular the fight against cigarette smuggling. increased taxes on these products, particularly in france, can distort competition within the eu and encourage smuggling of cigarettes from both member and non-member countries.
in writing. this text strengthens the protection of the financial interests of the european union by establishing the hercule iii programme for the period 2014-2020. it is important that the european union progresses towards an effective prevention of fraud, corruption and other illegal activities. it is therefore particularly interesting to offer specialised joint training for staff in national and regional administrations. such a proposal contributes to ensuring an equivalent level of protection throughout the european union.
in writing. i voted in favour of this text, which aims to continue the action taken by the european union in the field of the protection of the union's financial interests. one of the benefits of this measure is that it allows savings to be made through the collective acquisition of specialised equipment and databases for stakeholders. in addition, the provision of assistance to facilitate investigations and the setting up of joint investigative teams and crossborder operations are elements which i hope will make it possible to actively combat financial fraud.
in writing. i supported the report by my colleague monica luisa macovei on the hercule iii programme and protection of the financial interests of the european union, aimed at combating smuggling and fraudulent practices, particularly in the context of the cigarette trade. the report proposes to strengthen the cooperation mechanisms and investigative capacity of olaf (european anti-fraud office). the text was adopted by a very large majority with 644 votes in favour, 14 against and 12 abstentions. i'm very pleased with this adoption.
in writing. this report focuses on the hercule iii programme which promotes the protection of the eu's financial interests for the period 2014-2020. initially launched in 2004, the hercule programme focuses on three main areas: strengthening cooperation between anti-fraud actors, strengthening information exchange networks and providing operational and technical support to law enforcement agencies. it also aims to increase the number of measures to combat counterfeiting and smuggling of cigarettes. the programme has consistently proved its effectiveness and i believe that it is essential to continue it, particularly at a time when budgetary questions are central to the problems facing the member states. i therefore voted in favour.
in writing. i supported this text which strengthens the coherence of european legislation with the new institutional framework. it seems to me appropriate to seek to streamline the production of community statistics on trade in goods between member states, in particular by clarifying the definition of statistical value.
in writing. i voted in favour of the report by my colleague hans-peter martin on statistics relating to the trade in goods between member states. the text delegates to the european commission implementing powers for the adoption of certain measures, the communication of information by the customs administration, the exchange of confidential data between member states and the definition of the statistical value. the text will now enter the negotiation phase with the council and the european commission with a view to a final agreement. so i welcome this result.
in writing. the fight against wildlife crime requires coordinated global action by the highest political and enforcement bodies at national and international level, and the effective use of tools to strengthen law enforcement and criminal justice systems. this type of traffic is a danger to the environment and local communities. i therefore supported this text which also calls for all the member states of the european union to strengthen coordination in this area in order to put an end to it.

in writing. i supported the resolution calling for the fight against wildlife crime, which is often linked to transnational criminal organisations, drug traffickers and human traffickers. the resolution calls for stricter action by the authorities and greater cooperation with international organisations such as interpol. i therefore welcome the adoption of this resolution.
in writing. europe is an important market for poachers who take advantage of the non-harmonisation of european regulations on the protection of biodiversity to bring goods into the eu. wildlife crime includes acts of poaching, trafficking or possession of protected flora and fauna. these practices often lead to the extinction of species, damage biodiversity and cause serious damage to ecosystems. the resolution adopted therefore sets out guidelines to combat this form of crime. it was essential that the european union commit itself to combating wildlife crime and i therefore supported the resolution voted by the european parliament.
in writing. i voted in favour of the resolution on combating poaching and wildlife crime. as vice-president of the animal welfare intergroup in the european parliament, i am very much involved in issues of respect for biodiversity. poaching is now an activity of mafia-type criminal groups that take advantage of weak controls and law enforcement, especially in african countries, to expand their activities. interpol and the international fund for animal welfare have shown that the ivory trade is booming and that the european union is the world's leading destination market! in this text i have therefore called for the european union to introduce moratoriums on all imports and exports of elephant tusks and raw or processed ivory products until wild elephant populations are no longer threatened by poaching. i have also asked for more precise controls to be applied to imports of hunting trophies for a number of species, again with the aim of raising awareness among the european public of these issues.
in writing. i voted in favour of this european parliament resolution which highlights the issue of wildlife crime. the aim is to combat illegal wildlife trade, poaching and illegal harvesting, and trade in wildlife products. in 2013, over 41 tons of ivory from elephant poaching in africa and asia were seized - the highest amount in 25 years! the same is true of rhinoceroses, especially in south africa. not only is this trade unacceptable from the point of view of respect for animals, which are usually protected species, and the balance of ecosystems, but several international organisations, such as the united nations and interpol, have shown the link between the exploitation of wildlife and international organised crime. as the european union is the world's leading destination market for trafficking in human beings, it is time for the eu to put in place a coordinated legal framework to strengthen the fight against this real scourge. the setting up of a special committee within europol to deal effectively with this issue may be a first step in this direction.

author. - madam president, the question of environmental damage, which is of a very different nature from the whole subject we have just discussed, is becoming increasingly important. first, because of the irreversibility of the situation, we have entered the sixth extinction of species, and also because of the financial cost of this damage. i would remind you that the services provided by nature amount to 23 billion a year, or half of the world's gdp. environmental liability directive 2004/35 recognises environmental damage but excludes a number of categories, including environmental damage resulting from disasters related to oil spills at sea. in return, erika iii does not decide the issue. the creation of a complementary fund in 2003, which is in addition to the fipol, has resulted in the abandonment of a project to integrate ecological damage into the categories of damage compensated by this fund. the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the environment is protected. yet in the united states, environmental damage is recognized by case law, see the exxon valdez judgment. the european court of human rights recognises a right to a healthy and protected environment, see tătar v. romania. the court of justice of the european union has upheld the polluter pays principle as a general interest principle in the mesquer judgment in the erika case. finally, in this last case in which i had the honour of defending the french communes, the french court of cassation has recognised the existence of pure ecological damage. the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the community's environmental policy is not distorted by the fact that it is not able to meet the needs of the environment.

shortcomings of international law. the complex concept of liability in the event of disasters caused by shipwrecks affecting the seas and territories of the union needs to be defined more broadly. in france, the erika legal proceedings established the existence of pure ecological damage, which complements the economic, material or moral damage. at european and international level, the existing provisions are not sufficient to recognize purely ecological damage caused by natural disasters. the recognition of these rights is essential for the preservation of our territories and our seas, and in particular for the future of maritime activities in the context of the development of blue growth, which we all support. the convention on civil liability must also recognize that environmental damage is liable to compensation. the current regulatory framework only covers the cost of rehabilitation. in addition, the international compensation fund for oil pollution damage, fipol, established in 2003, should facilitate compensation for all types of damage. the procedures for using these funds should be simplified. for example, it would be useful for each member state to be able to work with fipol to establish lists of experts capable of speeding up compensation procedures. at european level, the scope of the environmental liability directive needs to be extended to take account of ecological damage to european marine waters. it could be invoked in cases where the convention on civil liability does not apply. finally, i think it is essential to set up a fund to supplement the fipol fund, which would be designed to repair the environmental damage. the cope fund, which was already proposed by the commission, was abandoned in 2003. it would have avoided the current legal vacuum.
for the greens/efa group madam president, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, today too often those who pollute and are responsible for ecological disasters are not the ones who pay. the polluter pays principle, which is at the heart of the european treaties, is not easily applied, as the judicial handling of these disasters shows. two examples have been widely cited. in france, for example, the erika case involved €143 million of public funds after the erika oil spill, whereas total was only fined €375,000. bp, which operates oil rigs in europe, has committed only one-twentieth of its market value to compensation for the unfortunately historic deepwater oil spill in the gulf of mexico. how can we compensate and make amends when we cannot prevent these natural disasters and the resulting ecological damage? europe has taken the lead by calling on member states to strengthen their criminal legislation and access to justice. but we must and can go further to force environmental offenders to face up to their responsibilities and make amends. at european level, the deadlock in the council over the directive on access to justice in environmental matters must now end and we must embark on a review of european regulation to make it more stringent and harmonised. in france, the erika case has set in motion the development of the law on the concept of pure ecological damage, but it is at european level that we can exert our full weight and ensure common and effective mechanisms, and that we must go further so that everyone assumes his criminal and civil responsibilities and so that cases such as the erika or the prestige really belong to the past.

in writing. i voted in favour of this resolution because i am very concerned by the revelations of several cases in europe of citizenship of a member state, and therefore european citizenship, being granted through investment programmes. it is true that the states remain - and must remain - the only sovereign ones to grant citizenship to their countries. but it can only be observed that these sales practices give rise to certain discrimination which is unacceptable, thus creating 'second-class citizens' between those who acquire nationality solely on the basis of their wealth and others who, despite a long-term presence in the territory of a member state, regular payment of taxes and compliance with integration measures, still too often struggle to obtain the famous 'sésame'. such measures also risk opening new avenues for money laundering through fraudulent activities abroad, as none of these investment incentives provide for controls on the origin of the money invested. we therefore need a european approach which, in my view, will prevent the possible drift of a system which, if it were to continue, would further undermine mutual trust between states.
in writing. how incongruous the decision of the maltese socialist government to offer the acquisition of maltese nationality for the modest sum of €650,000! apart from the fact that in my view naturalisation is not bought but earned, i regret that the maltese government has not considered the adverse effects of such a decision for the rest of the european union. malta's citizenship allows anyone with the necessary funds to move and reside throughout the eu. and it is a safe bet that naturalisation candidates will not only be virtuous entrepreneurs and lovers of maltese culture, history and cuisine! we should be wary of such decisions which could fuel crossborder crime networks. i therefore call on the maltese government to reconsider this decision in a spirit of calm and european solidarity and on all other member states which might have similar temptations not to take the same path.

in writing. the granting of citizenship is a matter of national subsidiarity and falls within the competence of the member states. however, by selling maltese citizenship, european citizenship is being auctioned off! this affects the european union as a whole. european citizenship comes with rights and duties. it is the expression of participation in our common project, and it is one of the pillars of the european union. the idea that this citizenship can be sold to the highest bidder is truly outrageous. the maltese government is betraying the trust that member states must be able to have in each other, the trust that we have been trying to build for several years.
in writing. this resolution condemns certain practices in the issuing of passports in eu member states. the report therefore opposes the sale of passports and residence permits by certain states. in the cases mentioned, citizenship is acquired either through investments, which are also suspected of concealing money laundering, or through outright sale without residence requirements (especially in malta). national identity cannot be a commodity. the false national consciousness of a state in the midst of decomposition cannot be used as a pretext for such a challenge to the civic status of the nation. i vote for this resolution condemning them.

the rapporteur. - madam president, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, the 2005 directive on unfair trading practices has proved its usefulness and effectiveness, with general principles according to which a practice can, on a case-by-case basis, be described as unfair or with a blacklist of practices still considered as such. however, we are facing new challenges today, major challenges arising from the development of new technologies. this is not only linked to the development of e-commerce, but also to the explosion of social networking and the proliferation of files of all kinds. this creates new unfair practices which also pose new challenges. i would simply like to mention three of them which are of particular concern and which have arisen from the rise of the internet. first, the confusion between independent information and advertising, for example in the form of dishonest comparisons of goods and services or, at the very least, maintaining ambiguity for dishonest purposes. i am thinking, for example, of the false comparators: those who charge companies whose products they recommend to buy by pretending to be objective. the second concern is false consumers and all the deception that can be made about the true identity of the author of a post on the internet, for example. unfortunately, it is not uncommon for certain traders to impersonate consumers in order to disseminate hidden advertising, and this is scandalous. third example, ip-tracking is also a practice that tends to spread. it involves artificially raising the price of a good or service each time a consumer visits the same web page from the same computer, giving them an artificial impression of urgency or scarcity that pushes them to buy immediately when there is no reason for it. the directive also faces other challenges: there are changes in behaviour and attitudes. with the growing awareness of the importance of sustainable development, greenwashing is in vogue. false environmental claims are on the rise. consumers may choose one product over another because they think they are making a better choice for the environment, or because they are willing to pay more for it, when in reality they are being duped. the report which will be put to the vote tomorrow draws the attention of the commission and the member states to these new practices. we want them exposed and fought. we believe that there is no need to amend the directive to that end because, by extension, it covers the cases i have just mentioned. however, there is one condition for the directive not to be amended: that it be properly applied, fully applied and fully applied. in other words, let the member states put the resources into it. i am thinking in particular of adequate resources but also of effective, proportionate and dissuasive sanctions against offenders. this is not sufficiently the case where, for example, the fines are lower than the abusive profits resulting from these bad practices. the commission must play its full part, obviously by monitoring the application of the directive, that is, by prosecuting those states which infringe the directive, do not implement it or do not ensure that it is applied properly. madam president, some people doubt the usefulness of europe, some say that it is concerned with things that are very far from the concerns of the citizens. i would like to conclude by saying to them that they are sometimes wrong. the directive on unfair trading practices is a concrete text example of what europe does well on a daily basis, provided, of course, that the states apply it correctly. we need to do even better in this area.
madam president, i thank the rapporteur for including the reference to ip-tracking in his report. this practice raises serious concerns among internet users and consumers and would, if proven, constitute fraudulent use of protected personal data. this practice is apparently growing in the air transport sector, where there is a severe lack of transparency in tariff policies. i therefore renew my call on the european commission to investigate the frequency of this practice and to adopt appropriate legislation if necessary.
in writing. the most vulnerable must be protected, and it is true that women without papers are particularly vulnerable. however, we cannot call for granting asylum to all undocumented women, simply because they do not have papers, or for creating specific rights for women who are in fact in an irregular situation. while we must protect women victims of human trafficking and do everything possible to combat their exploitation, we cannot reasonably expect that undocumented persons can lodge anonymous complaints against their employers. that is an irresponsible position which i cannot support in any way.
the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the directive is implemented. as rapporteur, i would like to begin by thanking the fictitious rapporteurs and all the political groups. it was thanks to our excellent cooperation that we were able to achieve unanimity in the committee on legal affairs on a sensitive subject such as copyright in the digital age. collective management companies are associations set up by artists and authors to defend their interests. it is the collective management societies that guarantee all european creators, not just the most famous ones, adequate remuneration for the use of their works and offer them social benefits. in the past, we have had to lament some examples of malfunction. from now on, collective management companies will have to comply with strict regulations. in addition, they will play their full role in european cultural policy and contribute to cultural diversity. we have achieved three objectives with this text. first, to guarantee the exercise of the rights of creators and artists. we have introduced greater transparency into the financial management of their accounts to avoid abuse or conflicts of interest. we have shortened the time for distributing the amounts collected. we have established the central role of the general assembly in the decision-making and control process so that the functioning of collective management societies is truly democratic. the second objective is to improve relations between collective management organisations, commercial users and citizens. relations between collective management organisations, broadcasters, radios and platforms now include reciprocal information obligations, in particular on the tariffs applied, which will simplify the licensing of copyright-protected works. if a platform like spotify gets a music catalog faster and cheaper, it means that european users will have easier access to the music of their choice. the third objective is to consolidate the digital single market. collective management societies will play a facilitating role in the internal market. instead of having to apply to 28 member states before being able to launch a pan-european online music service, the text will allow european platforms and start-ups to apply to a limited number of collective management organisations that will license the use of a global music repertoire. this is a real innovation. a spaniard or a greek living in brussels will have extensive, rapid and inexpensive access to the music of his country of origin. in conclusion, i note that copyright issues in the digital age have generated a lot of debate, but our work has changed the position. with this unanimous vote in the legal affairs committee, we have demonstrated to both the british conservatives and the swedish pirates our willingness to legislate in the general interest and in the interest of the digital single market. this directive is proof that copyright is easily adaptable to the digital world. it is proof that copyright is not a hindrance but an asset, a lever for growth and a source of jobs for the digital single market.
on behalf of the s&d group. mr president, the group of the progressive alliance of socialists and democrats welcomes the result achieved on the directive on collective management companies between parliament and the council. i think we should also thank the lithuanian presidency, which has facilitated the conclusion of this agreement. i would like to congratulate the european parliament on the very good work it has done in the run-up to this trilogue, thanks in particular to the very constructive and collaborative working method adopted by the rapporteur, marielle gallo. this apparently in size and form from one country to another, must be regarded as a moment of truth, to be dealt with in its entirety and with all its implications. it is quite clear that the main source of disillusionment, mistrust and rejection of the european project and, above all, of the work of the union's institutions, is the deterioration in living conditions and social status which has affected large sections of the population in most of the member states of the union and the eurozone. the emblematic figure, summing up all the negative and traumatic effects of the crisis, is the increase in unemployment, the dramatic rise in youth unemployment. it is therefore natural that the issue of a breakthrough capable of leading to the real revival of growth and employment which is considered by all parties to be essential and desirable has taken on a clear priority in the public debate and in the political debate. the commission has already made a number of proposals to this effect. the latter has been the predominant response to the sovereign debt crisis in the euro area and has favoured drastic measures to contain the deficit-to-gdp ratio, to rebalance, in forced stages, the public finances in each euro area country. in the face of the crisis, which had seriously jeopardized the financial sustainability of the eurozone countries, it was necessary to define and make binding a budgetary discipline which had been seriously lacking since the introduction of the single currency. you have therefore rightly contributed, as the parliament of the union, to the launching of important packages of measures to establish a strict framework for monitoring and coordinating budgetary decisions of the euro area member states. italy in particular has made considerable efforts and sacrifices in recent years, being subject to strong pressures on the financial markets because of the level of interest on the huge public debt accumulated in the previous decades. and even the marked improvement in this respect achieved in 2013 cannot dissuade us from the commitment to gradually and substantially reduce debt, a heavy burden that cannot be placed on the shoulders of the younger generation by the national ruling class. but the consequences of the severe stabilization measures adopted by the union and anchored to the maastricht parameters have had undeniably serious repercussions in terms of recession, falling gross product and domestic demand, especially in the countries called upon to make the greatest sacrifices, and this despite the courageous choices made by the ecb to combat speculation on the market for government bonds and to inject liquidity into the very tried economies of the euro zone. the change many people are calling for today cannot therefore be accompanied by demagogic irresponsibility and a retreat into situations of excessive deficits and debts. it must, however, reflect the awareness of a vicious circle which has now developed between restrictive policies in the field of public finances and the backwardness of the european economies, which are now at the crossroads between the first signs of recovery and the risks, if not of deflation, of substantial stagnation. breaking what has become, in many respects, a vicious circle - suggesting to an authoritative scholar like claus offe the image of a 'trapped europe' - is now essential, especially if we look at the condition of an entire generation today adrift. the same applies to a recovery in growth - if weak and not geared to specific objectives for the unemployed young people - which tends to offer poor and bad employment. in this connection, account must be taken of the radical technological changes that have taken place and are still taking place, and of the difficult competitive situation with large non-european economic areas. reforms of training systems and the labour market must therefore be carried out where they have not already been carried out, and investment must be made in knowledge, research and the preparation of the young workforce for new opportunities and forms of employment. sustained and qualified growth certainly requires structural reforms, but it also requires a revival of private investment and well-targeted public investment in the service of european and national projects. this requires beyond reference to rigidly defined parameters greater attention to the actual conditions of debt sustainability in each country and, in this connection, sufficient openness on the ways and timing of further financial rebalancing. the european parliament gave useful guidance in the wide-ranging resolution adopted on 12 december, which was inspired by the criteria of renewed solidarity within the union and in particular the eurozone. from the banking union, launched by the european council in june 2012, to an adequate budgetary capacity of the union based on specific own resources, to strong rules for the coordination of economic and national policies, ensuring greater cohesion between the economies of the member states: these and other elements are placed in your resolution in the context of a relaunch of the strategy of 'differentiated integration', with particular reference to enhanced cooperation in the field of economic and social policies. the resolution also makes reference to the unexplored potential of the existing treaties and to the need for future amendments to the treaties. in short, ladies and gentlemen, we are witnessing a profound change in the way the european union is and operates. the citizens-electors are not faced with a misleading choice between tired, rhetorical defence, on the one hand, of a europe which has shown serious shortcomings and distortions in the path of its integration and, on the other hand, destructive agitation against the euro and against the union. the european parliament has been a great help to the people of europe in the past, and it is a great help to the people of europe today. no, that's not the terms of the choice. president of the italian republic. - in fact, faced with a dramatic financial, economic and social crisis, the european institutions have moved with difficulty, amidst too many hesitations, divergences and slowness, but they have certainly moved in the direction of correcting previous behaviour. president draghi denied at a conference in berlin last november that there was any "lost decade". the euro area countries were encouraged, he said, to 'use the second decade of the euro to undo the mistakes of the first'. there is no rhetoric in these words, but a clear self-critical awareness. the euro was an innovation of historical value, but for too many years it remained a monkey's paw, devoid of essential complementarities, which can only be explained by anachronistic national closures and entrenchments in fields which, after the introduction of the euro, could not remain under national sovereignty. the gravity of the crisis has overcome many resistance and pushed strongly in the direction of greater integration. however, as regards the method and legal framework which prevail, there is no doubt that this has been done in the light of intergovernmental decisions and international agreements, outside the community framework, and that it will therefore be necessary, as parliament calls for and as the fiscal compact itself provides, to 'place the governance of a genuine economic and monetary union within the institutional framework of the union'. the question of a decisive strengthening of the democratic legitimacy of decisionmaking within the union is therefore: the commission's proposal for a directive on the protection of workers from the risks related to exposure to asbestos is a welcome step towards the creation of a european company. i would like to say that - in the crisis of popular consent which the european union and the integration process are suffering - there is the full weight of the economic and social malaise which the union has not been able to avoid, but there is also the weight of a serious political shortcoming, in various forms, in terms of information and involvement of citizens in shaping the union's policies and choices. and the change to be proposed to the electorate must therefore go beyond economic and social policies. the challenge must also go beyond these areas, to the forces that deny and oppose the project of european integration, its continuity and its necessary and possible renewal. a new era of economic growth, sustainable in all respects, is essential to rebuild confidence, but it is not enough to guarantee the democratic legitimacy of the integration process if it is not accompanied by new institutional and political developments in the life of the union. i think that those of us who believe in the cause of a united europe can prepare for the elections with serenity and confidence, as agents of change, all the more so if our design and experience are given their full face, their full richness, after having seen a reductionist, economic version prevail in recent years, with heavy technical connotations. the vision of what has actually been built in just over half a century has been attenuated and must be forcefully re-proposed: the community is not just a common market and an area of economic cooperation, but a community of values and, with it, a complex community of law, structured in the name of freedom and democracy. the european project has been continually broadened and the prospect of a common european vision and capacity for action in the field of international relations and defence and security has also emerged. the leaven of this unprecedented construction was the feeling of a very rich common culture: the european parliament has already expressed its views on the situation in the former yugoslavia. i draw the conclusion from all this that the foundations of the european construction are now so deep, that there is such a deep-rooted interconnection and interpenetration between our societies, our institutions, the social forces, the citizens and the young people of our countries, that nothing, nothing can bring us back. so there is empty propaganda and little credibility in the words of those who have taken a liquidating attitude towards what we have built over the past decades, from the europe of the 6 to the europe of the 28. how can one speak of the 'end of the european dream' and claim that this end could be avoided by abandoning the euro to save the union? the feasibility and traumatic consequences of such an abandonment are considered by some with disarming simplicity, nor do i see what the place should be and who the guarantors of such an unlikely exchange should be. in fact, despite the proliferation of catastrophic predictions of the imminent collapse of the euro in recent years, the institutions of the union and the most farsighted national political leaders understood that to safeguard the entire european project it was essential to defend the euro. but it was necessary to come to terms with the mistakes made, which were clearly due to the weakening of the common political will which had made that leap forward possible and which was to have presided over all the subsequent developments in european integration, together with the processes of german unification and the enlargement of the union. if what we are experiencing today, and which will be manifested in the forthcoming electoral contest, is - as i said at the beginning - a moment of truth for the cause of european unity and the future of europe, the decisive condition for success is a new, stronger and more decisive common political will, capable of conveying to the widest possible audiences the historical reasons and the new motivations of the european project. to convey them rationally and emotionally: it must be a message of passion, of deep feeling, like the one conveyed by the great images of the past decades. the one, for example, of françois mitterrand and helmut kohl, who hold hands and pay tribute to the dead in the terrible battle of verdun during the first world war. it has been written that these "two great europeans were imbued with the tragic sentiment of history": the european community is a community of nations, and the european community is a community of peoples, and the european community is a community of peoples. but i have never been infected by the fear that, in passing on political and governmental responsibilities to succeeding generations, the inspiration, the awareness, the common european political will, culminating in the unification of the entire continent on the basis of peace and freedom, might be dissolved. however, the question of whether these have not been dissolved and can find their strength in a different and new context is what must now be put to the test. of course, the motives of the european project have changed and they can speak well to the europeans of this century, to the europeans of today's world. yesterday the springboard of ending economic and political nationalism, which generates fatal conflicts, was a powerful springboard for winning consensus for the cause of european unity. the european parliament has been a very active participant in the process of european integration. europe as a whole has become smaller than other continents in terms of population, economic power and its role in the world balance, but if it can combine its forces more and more, it can continue to make its peculiar contribution to the historical development and future of world civilization. the new and exciting mission of a united europe is to bring to life, in the current of globalisation which could overwhelm us as european nations, our historical identity, our unmistakable cultural heritage, our example and model of supranational integration, of the community of law, of the social economy and of the market. but if this mission is to be shared by the peoples of our union and be carried out successfully, we need stronger european political cohesion, more convinced and determined european political leadership. thirty years ago, exactly thirty years ago here in strasbourg - let me remind you - altiero spinelli succeeded in making the european parliament express this leadership capacity with the draft treaty bearing his name. the opportunity was not seized then, but its constitutional inspiration has continued to live and count, also because its idea of a federal europe had nothing to do with the scarecrow stirred up by various parts of a centralized super-state. we have therefore come a long way since 1984, but there are still hard political battles to be won, if not against the possibility of aggressive nationalism, then certainly against the persistence of national selfishness and meanness, against narrow-mindedness, calculations of convenience and anachronistic conservatism, which are daily found in the national ruling classes. what is missing today, as helmut schmidt recently noted, is the "long-sightedness" of too many european leaders, who are not sufficiently aware of the decline threatening europe. the founding fathers and builders of the community were not only "imbued with the tragic sentiment of history", they were also the bearers of a bold and realistic vision of the future. and this can only be achieved today, or in the years to come, by a policy which finally becomes european, whereas, up to now, in a continent as interconnected as ours, politics has remained national, with its fatal limitations and widespread degeneration. a european policy, a european public space, european political parties, what is the political union of which we speak, if we do not make democratic political confrontation, competition between the different ideological currents and organized political forces, a reality on a european scale? this is a great leap forward and one on which the european parliament and its members have much to say, in close liaison with national parliaments and parliamentarians, in order to reach the broadest masses of citizens, involving them in a more informed and active political participation in the building of a more united, more democratic, more effective europe. the original and vital nucleus of european political parties is already at work in this parliament. it is here that the greatest sensitivities and skills are gathered on which to base a political message for the governance of europe to be shared with the citizens, beyond the code language and the complex technicalities of the union's governing institutions. it is in your hands, mr president, ladies and gentlemen, and in your hands in large measure, to give birth to and develop the political dimension of european integration in the new phase of development which it is about to enter. in writing. one of the successes of european integration that is too often underestimated is the free movement of workers. in practice, anyone moving to another member state to pursue a profession there should not encounter any administrative or daily obstacles as long as they comply with the rules of that state. however, this common market project is not complete. there are still obstacles. this is why we, as legislators, strive to make it easier for citizens and businesses to move, bearing in mind that simplification and facilitation should not be synonymous with permissiveness and complacency. the proposal to simplify the acceptance of certain public documents is a laudable objective if, as a corollary, controls are not relaxed. it is this caution that led me to support two amendments limiting the scope of the regulation under consideration to documents from the official registers of the member states only. the cross-border use of plain text and unofficial translations, as advocated in mr rapkay's report, increases the risks of misuse and identity theft. parliament must be more vigilant at every stage of the legislative procedure. the citizens would not forgive him for his lack of firmness.
in writing. i supported the report by my colleague bernhard rapkay to promote the free movement of citizens and businesses by simplifying the acceptance of certain public documents in the european union. the report aims to reduce the requirements for legalising official documents and to harmonise the rules relating to them, while maintaining a high level of legal certainty. the text was adopted by a very large majority, with 573 votes in favour, 62 against and 44 abstentions. i'm very pleased with this adoption.

in writing. about 12 million eu citizens reside permanently or temporarily in another eu country. free movement between member states is one of the fundamental rights of european citizenship and everything that can promote its smooth functioning must be supported. i therefore voted in favour of this report by the european parliament which simplifies the acceptance of public documents issued by one member state in another member state. this includes civil status documents and should simplify their mutual recognition between member states. this includes, for example, certified or uncertified copies of identity cards, diplomas, documents certifying a disability, etc. in the future, this simplification should be extended to a wider range of document categories. another important element is the need to establish standard, multilingual forms, which is already common practice for electronic social security forms. it is therefore a tool to simplify administrative formalities between member states and should help to reduce the difficulties that european citizens may encounter when moving within the union.

in writing. cases of insider dealing and market manipulation are currently not punished in the same way in europe, with some of the most serious financial crimes being punished by simple administrative sanctions with little deterrent effect. it is therefore in order to harmonize these very different practices in europe in the criminal field that i supported the report by my colleague mr mccarthy, so that in the future those responsible for a financial crisis who allegedly enriched themselves by manipulating the markets could be severely punished with a minimum sentence of four years in prison, with the member states free to propose even more severe penalties. these harmonised minimum rules will prevent financial crime offenders from exploiting the differences in regimes across the union and will make banks and financial institutions criminally liable, so that market abuse and its consequences will be taken more seriously. this text adopted at european level therefore brings a certain added value for our citizens.

in writing. - one of the causes of the current instability of the financial system is the misuse of inside information and deliberate market manipulation. if a small number of bankers have been able to exploit their own dishonest information to make lucrative deals, the financial crisis has shown how much the eu member states have paid for banks' willingness to take excessive and unjustified risks for profit. i voted in favour of the resolution on criminal sanctions applicable to cases where information which is not available to the general public is used for personal gain. an example of such an action might be a situation where shares in a company are bought on the basis of information known only to the company itself about the attempts of another company to buy it. when such information is released, the company's stock usually rises sharply, and those who previously bought it dishonestly reap large profits. in future, member states will have to impose a minimum of four years' imprisonment for the most serious market manipulation offences and a minimum of two years' imprisonment for disclosure of classified information to a market participant.
